statement: The Inca had no alphabetic writing system; khipu (knotted-cord records) are a genuinely disputed, live research question regarding whether they constitute a full writing system or a numerical/administrative tally device. Gary Urton, Signs of the Inka Khipu (University of Texas Press, 2003), proposed a binary-coding theory: seven binary construction choices per cord (fiber, spin, ply, color-order, attachment, knot-direction, pendant-attachment method) yielding an estimated 1,536 distinct cord identities with 12 base colors, placing khipu's theoretical information capacity in the range of early cuneiform. This binary-coding hypothesis remains actively debated; progress has been made deciphering numerical/administrative khipu content specifically (census, tribute, storehouse-accounting), but narrative khipu remain undeciphered. Colonial-era testimony (including Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala's own claim to have used khipu as a source for his 1615 chronicle) indicates khipu "initially detailed complex narratives but transformed during colonial times into simpler notational forms" — but no scholar has yet cracked a narrative khipu's content. Recent computational work (Jon Clindaniel, 2019 machine-learning analysis; Manuel Medrano and Ashok Khosla, 2021 network analysis) found cord-construction clustering correlating with geographic provenance and regional "grammatical" patterns suggesting regional "dialects," though full bibliographic details for these two papers were not confirmed in this research pass.
scholarly_disagreement: Whether khipu constitute a full non-alphabetic writing system capable of encoding narrative content (Urton's binary-coding hypothesis, extended by Clindaniel and Medrano/Khosla's computational work) or should be understood more conservatively as primarily numerical/administrative recording devices with undeciphered narrative potential remains genuinely unresolved in the field.

sources.citation: Urton, Gary. Signs of the Inka Khipu: Binary Coding in the Andean Knotted-String Records. Austin: University of Texas Press, 2003.
sources.author: Gary Urton

interpretations.position: Khipu constitute (or approach) a full writing system with substantial narrative-encoding capacity
interpretations.strongest_case: Theoretical information-capacity analysis places khipu's combinatorial complexity in the range of early cuneiform, and computational analysis has found real regional patterning consistent with an encoding system.

interpretations.position: Khipu are primarily numerical/administrative tally devices; narrative-encoding capacity is unproven and undeciphered

holders.name: General cautious/skeptical position within Andean studies, per convergent secondary sourcing

interpretations.strongest_case: No narrative khipu has actually been deciphered; the well-understood khipu content is confirmed numerical/administrative (census, tribute, storehouse accounting), and colonial testimony to prior narrative complexity is secondhand and unverifiable.
